summary: Defines the initial assignments of IPv6 Sub-Top-Level Aggregation Identifiers to the regional Address Registries. These were chunks of address space handed out early in IPv6 deployment. The scheme has since been superseded by other allocation practices.

eli5.summary: This is the first list of which big blocks of new-style Internet addresses went to which regional offices.

questions: early ipv6 address allocation to registries
subtitle: Early allocations of address space to regional Internet registries.

tldr.problem: IPv6 was being deployed with a new hierarchical address allocation scheme. Regional address registries needed to be assigned blocks of address space (Sub-TLA IDs) so they could allocate addresses to organizations.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board authorized IANA to divide a large IPv6 address block (2001::/16) into smaller blocks of 64 Sub-TLA IDs each and assign them to five regional registries (IANA, APNIC, ARIN, RIPE NCC) and reserve blocks for future assignments.
tldr.outcome: Each major region received an allocation of IPv6 address space immediately. The allocation scheme worked as a blueprint but was later superseded by other addressing policies. This document is published as a historical record of the initial strategy.

today: RFC 2928 is an Informational RFC from 2000 and is now a historical document. It describes the initial allocation of the 2001::/16 address block to regional registries. While these assignments remain in effect, IPv6 addressing policy has evolved, and today's allocations follow updated rules. Some blocks from this initial assignment (like 2001:db8::/32 for documentation) remain important for specific standardized uses.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, giving vastly more address space than IPv4's 32 bits. To manage this space, the IETF designed a hierarchical aggregation scheme. Addresses begin with a Format Prefix identifying the type (001 for global unicast), followed by a Top-Level Aggregation (TLA) ID, then a Sub-TLA ID.

This document was created in 1998 to advise the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) on how to allocate the first blocks of address space to regional registries. The Internet Architecture Board later requested that IANA delegate these assignments to the registries, and that is what happened. The registries have been using them since to assign IPv6 addresses to organizations.

The document is now published as a historical record of this initial allocation strategy.
sections.eli5: IPv6 has much more address space than IPv4. This document describes how the very first big chunks were divided up among regional offices.

sections.title: Background
sections.content:
The RFC 2450 Proposed TLA and NLA Assignment Rules specified a two-stage process: first allocate Sub-TLA IDs (smaller blocks) to registries, then the registries allocate those to organizations.

Sub-TLA IDs come from the special TLA ID 0x0001. The allocation uses 13 bits for the TLA ID (0x0001) and 13 bits for the Sub-TLA ID, which together form a /29 prefix when combined with the 3-bit format prefix. This creates large address blocks suitable for regional distribution.
sections.eli5: The two-step process lets IANA hand out blocks to registries, which then hand out smaller blocks to companies.

sections.title: Initial Assignments
sections.content:
Sub-TLA ID assignments are made in blocks of 64 IDs. The initial assignments are:

IANA (2001:0000::/29 - 2001:01F8::/29): Reserved for testing and experimental use to support activities like the 6bone (an IPv6 testbed network) and new exchange points.

APNIC (2001:0200::/29 - 2001:03F8::/29): Asia-Pacific region.

ARIN (2001:0400::/29 - 2001:05F8::/29): North America.

RIPE NCC (2001:0600::/29 - 2001:07F8::/29): Europe, Middle East, and Central Asia.

Remaining blocks (2001:0800::/29 through 2001:FFF8::/29) are reserved for future assignments. When a registry has assigned all Sub-TLA IDs in its current block, it can request additional blocks from IANA. The blocks assigned to a registry do not need to be contiguous.
sections.eli5: IANA kept some for testing. The other big regions each got their own blocks to assign to local networks.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
These assignments were the initial IPv6 address distribution in the early 2000s. The /29 prefix size (given in the RFC) was based on the address allocation model of that era.

Over the following decades, IPv6 deployment strategy and address allocation policies evolved significantly. Today's address allocation follows updated rules that differ from this scheme, and the Sub-TLA assignment model is no longer the primary means of IPv6 address distribution. However, addresses in the 2001::/16 block (particularly 2001:db8::/32 for documentation and 2001:20::/28 for testing) remain important for specific purposes.

This RFC is now maintained as a historical record of how IPv6 address allocation began.
sections.eli5: These were the first assignments, but IPv6 allocation rules have changed many times since then. Some of the address blocks are still used for special purposes.
